title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough — batching & KV cache (NovaPayments)
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked NovaPayments through the Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV caching. Main focus was on reducing per-token cost for conversational agents while meeting 200ms P95 latency targets. Discussed tradeoffs between aggressive batching, prefix caching hit rates, and model quantization. Action: AE to share benchmark sheet and preliminary pricing; SE to run a short KV cache feasibility check with NovaPayments sample traffic.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-15
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO - NovaPayments), Sofia Martinez (Head of ML), Daniel Cho (Infra Lead)

Summary (auto): walkthrough of Optimize recommendations focused on batching and KV/prefix caching; cost model examples applied to NovaPayments' chat workload; next steps: send benchmark spreadsheet, set up pilot test of KV cache, follow-up architecture session.

00:00 Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everybody, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya our SE. We'll run through our Optimize recommendations for batching and KV/prefix caching and then talk through numbers for your traffic. Marcus, Sofia, Daniel, thanks for coming on.
00:26 Marcus (NovaPayments): Yeah thanks — rough week but happy to be here. We're hoping to see where we can shave cost down without impacting latency for our customer support assistant.
00:35 Priya (Redwood SE): Great, we'll aim for concrete recommendations. Quick agenda: 1) baseline — what your current qps and tail latency look like; 2) batching & compile/kernels impact; 3) prefix vs KV cache and hit rate modeling; 4) cost model with example numbers; 5) security notes and next steps.
01:02 Sofia (NovaPayments): Quick callout — our SLA is 200ms P95 for web chat, and we have a mix of short context chats (avg 40 tokens) and longer threads for escalations.
01:15 Daniel (NovaPayments): infra-wise we're on GCP with VPC peering, and we require all logs to land in our SIEM — SOC2 in flight.
01:24 Alex: Perfect, that's helpful context. Priya, want to kick into batching principles?
01:28 Priya: Sure. So high level: batching increases throughput by amortizing kernel overhead, but it adds queueing latency. For your distribution — lots of short requests — small batching windows can give big cost wins. I want to show the console demo with two profiles: conservative latency SLO (200ms P95) and cost-optimized.
01:48 Priya: (screen) Here's a sample trace from a customer with similar traffic. You can see with continuous batching enabled we improve tokens/sec by about 2.3x, but the median latency moves from ~45ms to ~70ms; P95 is the region that matters for you.
02:12 Marcus: That 2.3x number — is that across mixed sequence lengths or just short seqs?
02:17 Priya: Mixed. It assumes our adaptive batching algorithm that groups compatible sequence lengths and honors KV cache warmups. For short sequences you often get larger relative wins because the kernel overhead is proportionally bigger.
02:31 Sofia: What about cold starts — if a user hits a long tail prompt, does batching wait and slow everyone else?
02:39 Priya: We do workload-aware batching: requests that would break the latency SLO are fast-tracked. Also can configure a max batching latency window, e.g., 10ms or 25ms, and also size caps. For your P95 target we'd probably set 10–15ms batching window plus a hot-path fastlane.
03:00 Daniel: That sounds reasonable. Now prefix/KV cache — how do those interact?
03:06 Priya: Two separate layers: prefix caching is storing recurring prompt prefixes (like system messages, user profile contexts) so we don't re-run the full context attention. KV cache refers to the per-session key-value cache for autoregressive decoding — we keep and reuse it across requests for the same session to avoid recomputing. They are additive.
03:26 Priya: (slides) If you have high prefix reuse — say templated prompts for support with variable substitution — your prefix cache hit rate could be 60–80%, which yields big per-token compute savings. KV cache is most valuable for multi-turn flows where you keep generating.
03:45 Sofia: Our reuse is moderate; templates for greetings and account lookup are reused a lot, but user messages are unique. So maybe 40–50% prefix hit?
03:55 Priya: That's still material. We'll model a scenario with 45% prefix hit and a session reuse that keeps KV cache active for ~3 turns on average.
04:06 Alex: Let's switch to the cost model. I've uploaded a small workbook we use — sharing link in chat. The model factors: model choice (fp16 vs int8), tokenization mix (prompt vs generation tokens), batching factor, prefix hit rate, KV cache reuse, and infra cost (GPU type).
04:26 Alex: For a baseline, imagine 10k daily concurrent users, avg 1.5 reqs/sec per active, average generation 60 tokens, prompt 30 tokens. With no caching and no batching we land at X tokens/sec and cost Y. With batching at 2.3x and prefix hit 45% plus KV reuse we reduce GPU-seen tokens by ~50% which yields ~45% cost reduction in the example.
04:52 Marcus: Can you show concrete numbers for our case?
04:56 Priya: Yep. (screen) Here is the workbook populated with your rough numbers: peak concurrent threads we set to 1,200, avg request size 90 tokens (prompt+gen), we model two GPU choices: A100 and L40-like; we run model at int8 quant to save memory and cost. 
05:18 Priya: With batching window 15ms, expected effective batching factor ~2.1 during peak. Prefix hit 45%, KV reuse 3 turns — net tokens executed by model drop by 48%, and cost per 1M user tokens drops from $Z to about 0.55*$Z. (Note: numbers redacted in call, will send sheet.)
05:42 Daniel: That int8 path — any change to latency? Quantized kernels actually help CPU/GPU throughput but sometimes increase decode latency a bit, right?
05:52 Priya: Right, generally int8 gives less memory and faster throughput; decode latency per token is slightly higher in some models but overall wall-clock for request usually decreases because more tokens fit in memory and batching improves. We'll run a small perf test to verify.
06:10 Sofia: Security question — with KV cache and prefix cache, where's data stored and encrypted? We need KMS integration and audit logs for cache access.
06:20 Alex: For Dedicated/Private deployments we store cache in customer VPC; we support KMS/HSM-backed encryption at rest and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. For Hosted we have encryption at rest and can offer customer-managed keys on enterprise plans. We'll include the security doc.
06:38 Marcus: Good. Also curious about cache invalidation when templates change or revocation.
06:44 Priya: We expose TTLs and eviction policies and provide hooks in the console to purge keys by namespace or prefix. You can tightly control TTLs and programmatic invalidation; we can also integrate a webhook to notify Redwood to evict if you change template versions.
06:59 Alex: Back to cost tradeoffs — another lever is routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical routes. For example, summary generation could use a smaller model; chat agent uses larger. That can be modeled in the workbook as route weights.
07:15 Marcus: Nice — default routing rules?
07:18 Alex: We ship with templates; you can do rule-based routing (by route, by latency SLO, by model quality tag). We'll help with initial set.
07:29 Priya: (screen) I want to show microbenchmarks. This is a recorded run on an L40-style instance: single-request model latency, batched throughput, and cache-hit case. See here: warm KV cache reduces end-to-end time for multi-turn flows by ~30% in this workload.
07:52 Daniel: Are these numbers reproducible on our on-prem stack?
07:57 Priya: The kernel paths are optimized across hardware but we do see variation. That's why we recommend a short pilot: run a week of traces from your traffic on our Dedicated test pool and we'll produce tuned batch windows and cache sizing.
08:12 Sofia: Ok, what's needed from our side for the pilot?
08:16 Alex: Ideally a 48–72 hour sample of request/response logs (no PII), anonymized prompts if necessary, and expected traffic shape. Also a contact on infra for VPC peering if you want to test Dedicated.
08:29 Daniel: We can do anonymized traces, yes. SIEM integration — we'll need some details for compliance.
08:34 Alex: We'll include SOC2/ISO docs and a checklist for SIEM forwarding.
08:39 Priya: Quick note on hit-rate modeling: small changes in prefix templating can swing hit rates a lot. For instance, normalizing user IDs into a slot increases prefix reuse dramatically. That's a low-effort change on your side with a big impact.
08:55 Sofia: Good call — we already have template placeholders for names but not for account IDs. We'll look into that.
09:02 Marcus: About rollout — we want to avoid regressions in quality. How do you recommend we test for hallucination or degradation when moving to int8 / caching?
09:10 Priya: We have an eval harness you can run with a golden set of prompts — compare generations pre/post. We also do drift/regression alerts tied to prompt sets and can block rollouts if quality drops beyond a threshold. We'll share the eval template.
09:23 Alex: Also can canary rule models per route, e.g., 10% traffic on quantized model, monitor quality and latency, then expand.
09:31 Marcus: Sounds good. Any other infra costs we should be aware of?
09:35 Priya: Network egress for embeddings or heavy attachments can add up. For typical chat it's minor. Also cache storage cost is typically small compared to GPU time, but KV caches for long-lived sessions can increase memory footprint — that's included in Dedicated sizing.
09:50 Daniel: For Dedicated, do you allow pre-warming capacity for peak days?
09:54 Alex: Yes, configurable burst pools and reserve capacity for known events, with SLA-backed routing.
09:59 Sofia: Let's go through the concrete next steps and owners.
10:03 Alex: Great. Recap: 1) Alex will send the populated cost/benchmark workbook and preliminary pricing; 2) Priya will run a feasibility perf run against a 48hr anonymized trace and return a tuned config; 3) NovaPayments will share anonymized traces and a point of contact for infra. Any additional items?
10:22 Marcus: Also would appreciate a short doc on prefix normalization best practices.
10:26 Priya: We'll include that in the packet.
10:29 Alex: Timeline: we'll aim to deliver the workbook and pricing by 2026-06-17, perf run results by 2026-06-22. Does that work?
10:36 Marcus: Yes that works.
10:38 (crosstalk) Sofia: Thank you, this was helpful.
10:42 Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the perf session.

(Transcript notes: occasional ASR errors, some proper nouns mis-transcribed — e.g., model names, GPU types — will attach original recording and the spreadsheet with exact numbers.)
